lessons.title: Biltong Basics: Spices, Vinegar, and Air-Drying
lessons.body:
Biltong is a traditional African cured meat made from beef, game, or ostrich. The key ingredients are coarse salt, brown sugar, coriander seeds, black pepper, and vinegar. For 1 kg of meat, use 20 g coarse salt, 10 g brown sugar, 10 g toasted coriander seeds (crushed), 5 g black pepper, and 100 ml brown vinegar (or apple cider vinegar). The vinegar creates an acidic environment that inhibits harmful bacteria while allowing beneficial enzymes to tenderise the meat. Salt draws out moisture and further protects against spoilage.

You will need a sharp knife, a mixing bowl, a drying rack (or hooks), and a well-ventilated space. Cut the meat into strips about 2 cm thick, 5 cm wide, and as long as you like. Trim off excess fat and sinew. Mix the dry spices together. Dip each strip into vinegar, then rub generously with the spice mix. Layer the spiced strips in a bowl, cover, and refrigerate for 12 to 24 hours. This curing step flavours the meat and starts the preservation process.

After curing, hang the strips to dry. In a dry, breezy climate, you can hang them outdoors under shade cloth or in a dedicated drying box. Air must circulate around each piece. Depending on thickness and humidity, drying takes 3 to 5 days. The biltong is ready when it is firm and dry on the outside but still slightly moist inside. If you prefer it drier, leave it another day. In humid climates, use a fan or a light bulb in a drying box to keep the air moving and prevent mould.

Store finished biltong in a paper bag or breathable container in a cool, dry place. It keeps for weeks. Never store in plastic, as trapped moisture causes mould. With practice, you can adjust spices to your tasteâsome add chilli flakes, garlic powder, or a pinch of bicarbonate of soda to soften the meat. Biltong is high in protein and perfect for snacks, hiking, or selling at local markets.

lessons.title: Making Beef Biltong: Step-by-Step from Raw to Dry
lessons.body:
Start with the right cut. Beef silverside, topside, or rump works best. Choose meat that is fresh, lean, and at least 2 kg. Ask your butcher to cut it into long strips with the grain, about 2 cm thick. Fat should be trimmed but not entirely removedâa little fat adds flavour. You will also need coarse salt, brown sugar, coriander seeds, black pepper, vinegar, and optional Worcestershire sauce. For 2 kg beef: 40 g salt, 20 g sugar, 20 g coriander, 10 g pepper, 200 ml vinegar.

Step 1: Toast coriander seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, then crush coarsely. Mix with salt, sugar, and pepper. Step 2: Pour vinegar into a shallow dish. Dip each meat strip into vinegar, ensuring full coverage. Step 3: Rub the spice mix into the meat on all sides. Place strips in a glass or plastic container, cover, and refrigerate for 24 hours. Turn the meat once after 12 hours. Step 4: Remove from fridge and pat off excess liquid with paper towel. Do not rinse.

Step 5: Hang the strips. Use stainless steel hooks or paper clips (sanitised) to hang meat in a drying box or a cool, dry room with a fan. Space them at least 5 cm apart. Ideal temperature is 15â20Â°C with 50â60% humidity. If humidity is higher, use a fan or dehumidifier. Step 6: Dry for 3 to 5 days. Check daily. The biltong is done when the outside is hard and dark, but the inside is still slightly pink and moist. For wet biltong (more moist), dry 3 days; for dry, 5 days. Step 7: Cut a piece to test. It should be firm but not rock-hard. If mould appears (green or black spots), discard affected pieces and increase airflow.

Once dry, slice thinly against the grain. Store in paper bags or cotton sacks in a cool, dark place. It keeps for 2â4 weeks. For longer storage, vacuum-seal and freeze. This method works for beef, game, or ostrich. With practice, you can scale up for a small business selling biltong at markets or to local shops.

lessons.title: DroÃ«wors: Spiced Dry Sausage from South Africa
lessons.body:
DroÃ«wors is a traditional South African dry sausage, similar to biltong but made with minced meat and spices stuffed into casings. It is a favourite snack and keeps well without refrigeration. The basic recipe for 2 kg of beef (or game) mince: 40 g coarse salt, 20 g brown sugar, 20 g toasted coriander seeds (crushed), 10 g black pepper, 5 g ground cloves, 5 g ground nutmeg, 100 ml brown vinegar, and 10 g baking soda (optional, for tenderness). You will also need natural sheep or hog casings, a sausage stuffer (or a funnel), and a drying rack.

Start by mixing the mince with all dry spices and vinegar. Knead well for 5 minutes until the mixture is sticky. Cover and refrigerate for 2 hours to let flavours blend. Soak casings in warm water for 30 minutes to soften. Rinse inside and out. Stuff the meat mixture into casings, making links about 30 cm long. Do not overstuff, or casings will burst. Tie ends with string. Prick small holes along the sausage with a sterilised needle to release air.

Hang the sausages in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. Ideal conditions: 15â20Â°C, 50â60% humidity, with a gentle breeze. If humid, use a fan or a drying box. Dry for 4 to 7 days. The droÃ«wors is ready when it is firm and dry but still slightly pliable. It should not be brittle. Cut a link to testâinside should be dark red and dry. If mould appears, wipe with vinegar and increase airflow. In very dry climates, 4 days may be enough; in humid areas, up to 10 days.

Once dry, store in paper bags or hang in a cool pantry. It keeps for 3â4 weeks. For longer shelf life, vacuum-seal and freeze. DroÃ«wors can be made from beef, kudu, springbok, or ostrich. Adjust spices to tasteâsome add chilli or garlic. This is a popular product for informal traders because it is lightweight, nutritious, and has a long shelf life. Always maintain hygiene: clean hands, tools, and surfaces to prevent contamination.

lessons.title: Using Game Meats: Kudu, Springbok, and Impala
lessons.body:
Game meats like kudu, springbok, and impala make excellent biltong and droÃ«wors. They are leaner than beef, with a distinct flavour. However, they require careful handling because game animals may carry bacteria. Only use meat from healthy animals, and process it quickly after hunting. If you buy game meat, ensure it comes from a licensed butcher. For 1 kg of game meat, use the same spice mix as beef: 20 g salt, 10 g sugar, 10 g coriander, 5 g pepper, 100 ml vinegar. Game meat benefits from a slightly longer curing timeâup to 36 hoursâto tenderise.

Kudu is a large antelope with dense, dark meat. It is best for biltong because its low fat content dries well. Cut strips 2 cm thick. Springbok is smaller and more tender; its meat is mild and slightly sweet. It makes excellent droÃ«wors. Impala is similar to springbok but slightly larger. For all game, trim off all fat and sinewâgame fat turns rancid quickly. Use vinegar generously to kill surface bacteria. Some hunters add a tablespoon of lemon juice per kg for extra acidity.

Drying game meat takes 3 to 5 days, similar to beef. Because game is lean, it dries faster and can become too hard. Check daily. If the outside is hard but inside still moist, it is perfect. If it becomes brittle, reduce drying time next batch. In humid climates, use a drying box with a fan. Game biltong has a stronger, earthier flavour than beef. It is prized in South Africa and Namibia. You can sell it at a premium price.

For droÃ«wors, mix game mince with beef fat (about 20% fat) to prevent dryness. Otherwise, the sausage will be crumbly. Use the same spices as beef droÃ«wors. Stuff into casings and dry for 4 to 7 days. Game droÃ«wors is a delicacy. Always label your product clearly if selling, and follow local food safety regulations. With practice, you can create a niche market for game biltong and droÃ«wors, especially among tourists and health-conscious customers.

lessons.title: Building a Drying Box for Humid Climates
lessons.body:
In humid climates, air-drying biltong and droÃ«wors is risky because mould grows quickly. A drying box solves this by controlling airflow, temperature, and humidity. You can build a simple box using plywood, plastic sheeting, or a large cardboard box. The box should be at least 60 cm wide, 60 cm deep, and 90 cm tall. You will need a small fan (computer fan or 12V fan), a light bulb (40W) for heat, a hygrometer (to measure humidity), and a thermostat (optional). Total cost: about R500âR800 ($30â$50).

Cut a hole at the bottom for the fan to blow air in, and another hole at the top for air to escape. Cover holes with mesh to keep insects out. Install the fan to circulate air upward. Place the light bulb near the bottom to provide gentle warmthâaim for 25â30Â°C. Too much heat cooks the meat; too little slows drying. Use a hygrometer to monitor humidity. Ideal humidity is 50â60%. If higher, add a small dehumidifier or increase airflow. If lower, place a bowl of water inside. Hang meat from a wooden dowel or stainless steel rod using hooks. Space pieces 5 cm apart.

Run the box in a dry, shaded area. Plug in the fan and light. Check temperature and humidity twice daily. Turn meat occasionally. Drying time in a box is 2 to 4 days, faster than outdoor drying. The box protects against rain, insects, and dust. It also allows you to dry year-round, even in rainy seasons. Clean the box after each batch with vinegar and water to prevent mould spores. Replace the light bulb if it burns out.

For a larger operation, you can build a walk-in drying room with a dehumidifier and exhaust fan. But for home or small business, a box is enough. Always test your first batch: if meat dries unevenly, adjust airflow. If mould appears, increase fan speed and reduce humidity. With a drying box, you can produce consistent biltong and droÃ«wors regardless of weather. This is essential for selling to customers who expect quality.

lessons.title: Packaging and Storing Biltong for Long Shelf Life
lessons.body:
Proper packaging and storage are critical for biltong and droÃ«wors. Even fully dried meat can spoil if exposed to moisture, air, or pests. The goal is to keep it dry, cool, and dark. For short-term storage (up to 4 weeks), use paper bags, cotton sacks, or breathable containers. Never use plastic bags for storageâtrapped moisture causes mould. If you must use plastic, ensure the biltong is bone-dry and add a desiccant packet. For longer storage (3â6 months), vacuum-seal portions and keep them in a cool, dark place or freezer. Vacuum sealing removes air and prevents mould.

For selling, packaging must be attractive and legal. Use food-grade paper bags with a clear window, or vacuum-sealed pouches. Label with product name, ingredients, weight, production date, and expiry date. In South Africa, you need a certificate of acceptability (COA) from your local municipality to sell processed meat. Check your country's regulations. For informal markets, simple paper bags with a sticker are often acceptable. Always wear gloves when handling finished biltong to avoid contamination.

Store biltong in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. Ideal temperature is below 20Â°C. If you live in a hot, humid area, keep it in the fridge or freezer. Biltong can be frozen for up to 6 months without losing quality. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature. DroÃ«wors can be hung in a cool pantry if humidity is low. If it becomes too dry, it will harden; if too moist, it will mould. Check stored products weekly for signs of mould (green, black, or white fuzzy spots). If mould appears, discard the affected piece. Do not just cut it offâmould can spread invisible spores.

For a small business, invest in a vacuum sealer (about R1000âR2000) and a digital scale. Package in 50g, 100g, and 200g portions. Offer different flavours (original, chilli, garlic). Store in a cool room with a dehumidifier if possible. Keep records of production dates and batch numbers. This ensures you can trace any issues. With proper packaging, your biltong can reach customers far from your location, increasing sales and reducing waste.

quiz.q: What is the main role of vinegar in biltong making?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar creates an acidic environment that inhibits bacteria and also helps tenderise the meat.

quiz.q: How much coarse salt is recommended for 1 kg of meat in biltong?

quiz.q: Which cut of beef is best for biltong?

quiz.q: What should you do if mould appears on drying biltong?
quiz.explanation: Wipe with vinegar, discard badly affected pieces, and increase airflow to prevent further mould.

quiz.q: How long does beef biltong typically take to dry?
quiz.explanation: Depending on thickness and humidity, biltong dries in 3 to 5 days.
